idiom_name: one immutable state value + intent values + pure reduce(state, intent) + single render(state)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the feature one state object that describes everything the screen can show (including loading, empty and error variants); accept user actions only as intent values that name what the user wants to do; apply them in one pure function reduce(state, intent) that returns the next state (and the input unchanged for intents it does not handle) and is the only code allowed to create state; publish each new state to a single render(state) entry point; and run I/O, timers and persistence outside the reducer, feeding their results back as further intents. Model one-shot work (navigation, toasts, analytics) as effects with their own delivery channel rather than as state fields, keep the state serializable so it can be restored, logged and replayed, and serialize intent handling through one thread or actor so transitions cannot interleave.
code_sketch:
state = initial
loop:
    intent = view.next_intent()          # user input as data
    state = reduce(state, intent)        # pure: (State, Intent) -> State
    view.render(state)                   # one output renders the whole screen
# effects run outside reduce and feed their results back as intents
pitfalls: Letting the view keep its own copy of the state (or mutate widgets outside render) recreates the parallel-state problem the loop removes.
Reducers that perform I/O or read clocks and randomness make transitions non-deterministic and untestable; keep them pure and put effects at the boundary.
Sending one-shot events (navigation, toasts) through the state stream replays them whenever the state is re-emitted or restored; give them their own effect channel.
One reducer serving several screens, or a mutable state handed to the view, undermines the single-owner rule; scope one loop per feature and publish only immutable snapshots.

Wrong move: Treat every screen as one giant reducer and state tree -> boilerplate and coupling overwhelm simple features -> instead scope MVI to feature flows with non-trivial transitions and use a lighter local state holder for small widgets.

Wrong move: Process asynchronous intents concurrently without a stale-result policy -> an older response can overwrite newer state -> instead serialize intent handling or cancel and ignore stale work explicitly.
